This is a look at my own personal experience, and does not reflect the thoughts of everyone at the company or in the community.Â

I'm the lead developer of HAProxy and a member of the Linux Kernel security team. Over the last few months, I've seen hundreds of AI-assisted "security reports" almost always following the same pattern: someone submits "here's a bug" with no reproducer and no patch. It has just become routine to deal with incomplete reports because the reporter often has no idea what the LLM thinks it found.

Yet this is not an LLM problem at all. A few months ago, a trusted colleague who had access to Anthropicâs most powerful model, Mythos, used it to analyze HAProxy. That experience gave me confidence in the model's actual capabilities and the results when paired with human expertise.

## Reports we can't use, a model we can't get

To help address the flood of low-value AI reports, I documented the threat models for both Linux Kernel and HAProxy so LLMs could better calibrate severity and stop wasting everyone's time on issues that either can't happen or have no real-world impact. This has noticeably reduced the rate of boring reports on both projects (not enough yet on Linux, where some researchers are still focused on outdated versions lacking the documentation updates).

Around the same time, the Linux Foundation provided me with a six-month subscription to Claude Max with 20x usage. It took me a little while to adapt to working in agentic mode, but thatâs OK now. The product itself is impressive, genuinely powerful, and clearly still improving. Its ability to work within a very large context window that covers the entire code area under scrutiny makes it feel almost as if it's seeing through walls. Unfortunately, that access didn't include Mythos, which remains subject to additional access restrictions.

For instance, access to models with true cyber âdefenseâ capabilities has become draconian unless you know the ârightâ people. Even though I completed Anthropic's Cyber Verification Program (CVP) hoping it would solve this, it still grants no access to Mythos. I reached out to contacts at Anthropic requesting access; the request was apparently deemed legitimate, but still nothing came of it. Anthropic continues to mature its program, but each time they change the process, it means starting over with a greater administrative burden, with no certainty of receiving access for legitimate defensive work. I was told the same wasnât much better for OpenAIâs Daybreak program, where our Security team had been rejected twice in recent months without explanation prior to their CVP updates.

Still, this streamlined workflow allowed us to work more efficiently and merge about one-third of the proposed fixes after reworking them to better align with our standards, preferences, and long-term goals.

## Safeguards fire at the wrong moment

Following that, the release of Fable 5 initially seemed promising, but it introduced nasty safeguards that render it unsuitable for low-level development where performance and security matter. They trigger constantly. There's no realistic scenario in which you could scan your code for security issues, let alone read a security report with Fable; it instantly refuses and demands downgrading to Opus 4.8. Apparently, the word "bug" in the prompt combined with reading C code is enough to instantly flag everything as cybersecurity work that shouldn't proceed. To date, I still have no idea whether anyone has successfully used this model, or for what purpose. Certainly not low-level development, at least.

The subsequent arrival of Opus 5, followed by 5.5, delivered impressive improvements. They really feel like tools designed to help the developer, almost like a skillful coworker. You can delegate long and complex tasks without worrying what youâll get at the end; theyâre well organized, thoughtful, and even tend to anticipate some requests by spontaneously proposing nice extras. The safeguards trigger much less often than Fable but still too frequently to be reliable for developers writing secure code that needs to be verified (otherwise itâs not secure, is it?). At least they can find bugs now, and occasionally produce a working reproducer. But often when you already have a reproducer, they blatantly refuse to study the root cause of the bug!Â

When refusal happens, the approach that seems to work most of the time is to kill the session and restart from scratch, trashing whatever upset the model in its context, hoping the different initial random seed will steer it away from emitting the same token sequence that triggered the same safeguard at the cost of more tokens spent. Sometimes it takes 3-4 attempts or I have to accept a downgrade to Opus 4.8 and wait for ages for it to figure out a reproducer. Overall, the capabilities of these models remain pretty compelling despite this annoyance.

At the time, I didn't notice any meaningful difference in blocking rates between my work account (which didnât yet have any security access) and the validated CVP account I had through the Linux Foundation, leaving me unconvinced that the latter added any value.

## Access goes to the people doing the least work

Then came this odd turn: Anthropic published what amounted to an advertisement for their strongest competitor, GLM 5.3. In fairness, it wasn't meant as an ad; they were complaining about how competitors avoid annoying users with safeguards like Anthropic does in their long war on open weights which no longer fools anyone . But for those dealing with stubborn Opus or Fable refusals all day long, this lands very differently: that's exactly what they want! It made me curious enough to test GLM 5.3 myself. True, it does find bugs, runs faster, and costs less. On a first pass, it found roughly half the bug candidates Opus 5.5 found, but it also caught at least one real bug that Opus missed. Probably just need to run it twice, and at a fraction of the cost too.

Last month, Anthropic announced (with a surprising greeting image indicating that their marketing people were not on the internet before 2004) an "improved Cyber Verification Program" (CVP), which still doesn't fix anything, and is probably even making things worse for Open Source developers and maintainers without access to corporate resources. Individuals can only access the "defense" tier, which, according to Anthropicâs own graph scores, performs extremely poorly at discovering bugs and, at least in my own testing, appears identical to what I currently have on my personal account. Higher tiers are reserved for security professionals, meaning people who make a business of harassing open-source maintainers with pointless, unexploitable reports and then demanding CVEs to measure their relevance against competitors.Â

See the problem? They're giving more access to those causing harm while offering nothing better to the people doing the actual work of reading long and complicated reports, reproducing issues, validating them, issuing fixes, authoring descriptive commit messages and porting to maintenance branches. Anthropic is magnifying the burden on the Open Source community instead of helping.Â

Open Source maintainers should get prepared for an influx of reports, some good, some bad, but forcing them to do even more painful bug-fixing work for free while others are building their companyâs reputation on top of their efforts.

## What developers actually need

Let me clarify what most developers actually need, as confirmed through discussions with several other OSS maintainers:

- Scan their code themselves to find bug candidates in specific areas

- For each bug, try hard to write a reproducer proving the bug is reachable in existing code without cheating by modifying it. A good reproducer is one you can reuse later, when backporting fixes to maintenance branches, to verify that the fix was needed and worked there as well.

- For each bug, write one or preferably several fix candidates from the same session's context, while that context is still rich enough to understand all the interactions that led to the bug being flagged, and explain why those fixes would durably work.

- Eliminate false positives identified by the steps above (writing fixes really sorts them out).

- Write tests to ensure the fix didn't introduce regressions, and check for other potential bugs in the same class.

What most developers do not need:

- To write weaponized exploits (e.g., shellcode injection)

- To penetrate running systems and hop from component to component

- To attempt privilege escalation

- To exfiltrate confidential data

- To affect data integrity

- To spend time triaging and reviewing totally disorganized reports about arbitrary code locations that are difficult to organize and dispatch to maintainers

The current poorly tuned (or designed) safeguards stop maintainers at step one, while all the other capabilities remain freely available to paid customers who continue making a business of selling exploits and pissing everyone off.
